summary: This standards-track document defines a YANG data model for managing network interfaces, covering both configuration and system state. It is meant as a generic base that interface-type-specific models can extend. It is written to work with the Network Management Datastore Architecture.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8343 defines a common data model for naming, configuring, and monitoring network interfaces. Other models can add details for specific interface types.

subtitle: A YANG model for configuring and monitoring network interfaces in one common structure.

tldr.problem: Network management systems need a consistent way to identify, configure, and monitor interfaces across devices and interface types.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-interfaces YANG module defines a list keyed by interface name, with configuration, read-only status and counters. Interface-specific modules can add their own data.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8343 obsoletes RFC 7223 and moves operational state into the /interfaces tree to support NMDA. It deprecates /interfaces-state.

today: RFC 8343 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2018. It obsoletes RFC 7223 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. RFC 8344 builds on this model.

sections.title: Why a Common Interface Model
sections.content:
Network interfaces are used by many Internet protocols, so management systems need a shared way to identify and monitor them. RFC 8343 defines a YANG model with both configuration and operational state, including counters.

The model is designed to be extended by interface-type-specific models and conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA). It obsoletes RFC 7223; operational data now lives in the /interfaces tree, while /interfaces-state is deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: This model gives management systems a shared way to describe network interfaces. It combines configuration with information about each interface's current state.

sections.title: Model Design Objectives
sections.content:
The model is intended to be simple to map to existing device data and usable directly by new implementations. Interface references should be simple, and the mapping to the ifIndex value used by SNMP must be clear.

The model covers physical and logical interfaces, supports configuring an interface before its hardware is present, and represents interfaces layered over or combined with other interfaces. It also includes read-only traffic counters.
sections.plainLanguage: The model aims to work with existing devices and new systems. It also covers physical interfaces, virtual interfaces, interface relationships, and traffic statistics.

sections.title: The Interface List
sections.content:
The ietf-interfaces module contains a flat list at /interfaces/interface. Each entry is identified by a unique name and has a required type. Configuration includes a description and enabled setting. Read-only values include operational status, last-change time, physical address, speed, and counters.

The oper-status field uses seven values, including up, down, testing, dormant, not-present, and lower-layer-down. Other YANG modules should use the interface-ref type to refer to an interface by name.
sections.plainLanguage: Each interface has a name and type, along with settings and read-only status. The model also provides counters for traffic, errors, and discarded packets.

sections.title: System-Controlled and User-Controlled Interfaces
sections.content:
A system-controlled interface appears or disappears when the system detects hardware or enables a function. A user-controlled interface exists because someone added explicit configuration, such as a VLAN interface.

When a system-controlled interface appears, the device tries to apply intended configuration with the same name and a matching type. Features named arbitrary-names and pre-provisioning indicate whether a server supports arbitrary user names and configuration for hardware not yet present.
sections.plainLanguage: Some interfaces appear when hardware or system features are present. Others exist because an administrator configured them.

sections.title: Interface Layering and Extensions
sections.content:
The generic module does not define how one interface is configured on top of another. Interface-type-specific modules define those settings and use interface-ref to name the lower interface. A bonding model, for example, can identify the physical interfaces that form a logical interface.

The generic model exposes the resulting relationships through read-only higher-layer-if and lower-layer-if lists. Type-specific modules can augment the interface list with settings that apply only when an interface has a particular type.
sections.plainLanguage: Separate models define how one interface uses another. The common model then reports which interfaces sit above or below each other.

sections.title: Relationship to the IF-MIB
sections.content:
On devices that implement the IF-MIB, an operational interface entry typically maps to an IF-MIB entry. The if-index leaf carries its ifIndex value. The RFC maps fields such as name, type, status, and counters to corresponding IF-MIB objects.

Not every IF-MIB object is represented in this model. For example, MTU is left to interface-specific models. The YANG model provides 64-bit octet and packet counters.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices that also support the older IF-MIB can map many of its interface fields to this model. Some details, such as MTU, belong in interface-specific models.

sections.title: Protecting Interface Configuration
sections.content:
The model is accessed through network management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. NETCONF must use SSH as its secure transport, and RESTCONF must use TLS. The NETCONF access control model can restrict which users may read or change data.

Unauthorized changes to the interface list or its enabled setting could cause a device to stop processing packets it should receive. The RFC registers the module's XML namespace with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: Only authorized management clients should change interface settings. Turning off an interface can stop the device from receiving and processing packets.
